name: Duty cycle
seoDesc: Duty cycle: work out period (T) from the pulse width and the pulse power (peak). A free other calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Duty cycle calculator turns the pulse width, the pulse power (peak) and the duty cycle into period (T). It suits whatever you happen to be working on. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Duty cycle calculator work?
sections.html:
The Duty cycle calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports period (T) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the find the duty cycle); then you type in the pulse width (PW), the pulse power (peak) (Pp) and the duty cycle (D).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as with time and with power. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in seconds. The unit chip switches it to any of the 27 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in watts. The unit chip switches it to any of the 21 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in percent. The unit chip switches it to any of the 6 supported units.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Duty cycle calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Period (T)=pulse width (PW) ÷ duty cycle (D)
Duty factor (df)=duty cycle (D)
Duty factor (df)=average power (P̅) ÷ pulse power (peak) (Pp)
Pulse energy (E)=pulse power (peak) (Pp) × pulse width (PW)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Find the duty cycle set to With time, Pulse width (PW) = 10 sec and Duty cycle (D) = 10 %. The calculator returns Period (T) = 100 sec and Duty factor (df) = 0.1.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Period (T) = 100 sec and Duty factor (df) = 0.1 should be roughly the size you expected from Find the duty cycle set to With time and Pulse width (PW) = 10 sec.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in seconds, and convertible to any of the 27 units on that chip.
  • A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.
  • Shown in watts, and convertible to any of the 21 units on that chip.
  • Shown in joules, and convertible to any of the 33 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Time, opening in seconds
  • Time, opening in seconds
  • Power, opening in watts
  • Power, opening in watts
  • %, opening in percent
  • Energy, opening in joules

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Duty cycle calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the pulse width, the pulse power (peak) and the duty cycle — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Duty cycle calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns period (T), derived from the pulse width, the pulse power (peak) and the duty cycle. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Duty cycle calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the pulse width, the pulse power (peak) and the duty cycle, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter pulse width (PW) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Pulse width (PW) opens in seconds and the chip beside it offers 27 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Period (T) = 100 sec. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Duty cycle calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
